title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: one life, three tenses, one opinion

questions.prompt: Complete the three gaps in this short paragraph: "Karim Bouzid ___ his first restaurant in 2011. He ___ two more since his brother joined him, and today he ___ forty people."

options.text: opened ... opened ... employs
opened ... has opened ... employs
has opened ... has opened ... employs
opened ... has opened ... has employed

questions.explanation: "in 2011" is a finished past date, so the first verb is the simple past; "since his brother joined him" opens a period that runs up to now, which calls for the present perfect; and "today" marks a fact that is still true, which takes the present simple: opened ... has opened ... employs. "has opened ... has opened ... employs" keeps the present perfect next to 2011, which a finished date kills. "opened ... opened ... employs" closes a count that is still open. "opened ... has opened ... has employed" turns a fact that is true today into a career total. The classic mistake is to pick one past tense and use it for the whole paragraph.

questions.prompt: Your classmate says that a singer should accept every interview request. You do not share that opinion. Which reply sounds the most natural in English?

options.text: I am not thinking it is a good idea.
I don't think so it is a good idea.
I don't think it is a good idea.
I think it is not a good idea.

questions.explanation: English prefers to negate the first verb, so the natural reply is "I don't think it is a good idea." "I think it is not a good idea." is understood but heavy, "I am not thinking it is a good idea." puts a verb of opinion into a continuous form, and "I don't think so it is a good idea." glues a whole clause onto "I don't think so", which is already a complete answer on its own. The classic mistake is to move the negative word for word and leave "think" positive.

questions.prompt: Read this portrait, then complete two lines of his identity card, place of residence and marital status: "Everybody in the stadium still shouts his first name, Tarek, but on his papers he is Tarek Mansouri. He was born in Nabeul in 1988 and played for three clubs before a knee injury ended his career in 2017. He now trains the young goalkeepers of a small club in Sfax, where he moved with his wife that same year. He has won two youth cups since 2019, and he says he sleeps better now, although he earns less than before."

options.text: Nabeul, and he is married.
Sfax, and he is married.
Nabeul, and he is single.
Sfax, and he is single.

questions.explanation: The text never writes the words "residence" or "married": both lines hide behind verbs. "He now trains the young goalkeepers of a small club in Sfax, where he moved with his wife" gives the two of them at once, so the card reads Sfax, and he is married. The classic mistake is to copy the place of birth and answer "Nabeul, and he is married", but he left Nabeul in 2017. "Sfax, and he is single" ignores "with his wife", and "Nabeul, and he is single" misses both clues.

questions.prompt: Which form fits the gap, and for which reason? "Leila ___ for the same newspaper since 2015."

options.text: works, because her job has not changed
worked, because the starting point is dated
has worked, because the event is over and dated
has worked, because the period runs up to now

questions.explanation: "since 2015" gives a starting point and the period is still open today, so the answer joins the right form to the right reason: has worked, because the period runs up to now. "has worked, because the event is over and dated" keeps the same form for a reason that would in fact call for the simple past. "worked, because the starting point is dated" closes in the past a period that has not ended, and "works, because her job has not changed" reads the sentence as a habit when it counts the years. The classic mistake is to pick the form by reflex and never check the reason behind it.

questions.prompt: Read this exchange. Rania: "What do you think of the new sports channel?" Sofien: "I'm still thinking about it. I have only watched it once." What does Sofien mean?

options.text: He has not decided what he thinks yet.
He is sure that the channel is very good.
He watches the channel every single evening.
He would like to work for the channel.

questions.explanation: "still" plus the -ing form says the work is not finished, and "I have only watched it once" says why, so the answer is: He has not decided what he thinks yet. "think about" here means turning something over in your head, which is exactly what somebody does before a verdict, not the verdict itself. "He is sure that the channel is very good." gives the judgement he has just refused to give, "He would like to work for the channel." reads a wish into the answer, and "He watches the channel every single evening." contradicts "I have only watched it once". The classic mistake is to hear "thinking about it" as an opinion, when it says the opinion is not ready.

questions.prompt: Read this interview with the photographer Rym Gharbi. Journalist: "You left engineering for photography. Any regrets?" Rym: "None at all. I studied engineering because my parents wanted a safe job for me, and I worked in a factory for four years. I sold my first photograph to a magazine in 2013." Journalist: "Is it hard to live from your pictures?" Rym: "It was, at the beginning. I have published in eleven magazines since 2016, and next month I fly to Kenya for a new series. I earn enough now, but I have never asked the press to write about me." True or false: Rym has never worked outside photography. Choose the verdict together with the words of the text that prove it.

options.text: True — "I worked in a factory for four years."
True — "I sold my first photograph to a magazine in 2013."
False — "I worked in a factory for four years."
False — "I sold my first photograph to a magazine in 2013."

questions.explanation: Rym spent four years in a factory before photography, so the statement is wrong, and a verdict is only worth the proof that comes with it: False — "I worked in a factory for four years." The very same words placed under "True" claim the opposite of what they prove, and both answers built on "I sold my first photograph to a magazine in 2013." only date the beginning of her photography instead of showing what she did before it. The classic mistake is to answer with the verdict alone, or to justify it from your own head instead of the text.
